h1: Nugget hops for bittering with a herbal flavour on top
title: Nugget Hops for Herbal Bittering | Craft Beer School
desc: Nugget hops for professional brewers: alpha range, herbal and woody character, a bittering calculation for 1,000 litres, storage in heat and substitutes.
teaser: Nugget is the bittering hop that does not apologise for itself. It adds a herbal, resinous edge that a neutral hop would not.
standfirst: Nugget is a high alpha American hop that has bittered beer for decades. It is cheap to use because little goes a long way. What is left in the glass is herbal, woody and a little spicy. Used well it gives a pale ale or a stout a backbone. Used carelessly it adds a coarse edge.
sections:
Nugget is an American high alpha variety released in the early 1980s from a US public breeding programme. Brewers buy it for bittering. Alpha acid commonly runs from about 11 to 15% depending on the crop year, so always calculate from the lot analysis on the certificate and never from a textbook figure.

Its oil profile is heavy and herbal. Descriptors are woody, resinous, green and a little spicy, sometimes with a hint of dark fruit. Those oils survive a 60 minute boil only in small amounts, so the character in a finished beer is a faint herbal note in the finish rather than a hop aroma.
Where it earns a place in the grist and the kettle

A hop that adds a trace of herb to the finish fits beers with some malt weight to carry it. English-style pale ales, ambers, porters and stouts suit it well. It also works as a workhorse bittering hop in an IPA when the late hops provide the aroma. In a clean pilsner, where nothing hides the bittering charge, many brewers prefer a more neutral hop. A softer option is in our guide on Perle for herbal bittering in German lagers.

Bitterness quality is the real question. High alpha hops can taste coarser than low alpha noble types at the same IBU, partly because of the balance of alpha acid fractions. Nugget is generally considered clean enough for most ales, but taste the beer before you commit it to a lager.

Work out the weight from the lot analysis. Here is an example for a 1,000 litre batch at 40 IBU with Nugget at 13% alpha and a utilisation of about 25% for a 60 minute boil at moderate gravity:

grams = IBU x litres / (alpha fraction x utilisation x 1,000) = 40 x 1,000 / (0.13 x 0.25 x 1,000) = about 1,230 g.

That is roughly 1.2 kg of pellets for the whole batch. Your own kettle geometry, gravity and boil vigour change the utilisation, so treat 25% as a starting point and adjust once you have measured IBU in the finished beer. Our guide to Warrior for clean high alpha bittering uses the same calculation for a different hop.
The floor detail: pellet storage in heat

High alpha hops store reasonably well, but they are not immortal. Oxygen and warmth degrade alpha acids and the oils. A bag opened in a store room at 35 °C and left half full will lose strength noticeably within weeks.

Keep pellets in sealed, oxygen barrier foil packs in a cold room at around 0 to 4 °C. When you open a pack, use it fully or flush with inert gas and reseal. Mark the open date on the bag. If your lot analysis is old, test or adjust the alpha figure down before you calculate. A 10% loss in alpha means an under-bittered beer unless you correct for it.

For most ales, add the bittering charge at the start of the boil once the wort is boiling vigorously. A single addition at 60 minutes is enough. If you want a smoother, more rounded bitterness, move a quarter of the charge to 20 or 30 minutes rather than boiling it all at once, accepting a lower utilisation.

Some brewers add Nugget in the last ten minutes of an English-style ale for its herbal note, but remember that the same weight gives much less bitterness. Check the IBU you intend, because late additions of a high alpha hop can change the balance more than you expect.
Substitutes when you cannot get it

If Nugget is out of stock, Magnum is the cleanest swap for pure bittering. Columbus or a similar resinous high alpha hop gets closer to the herbal edge. For something fruitier and cheaper, our guide on Bravo for fruity high alpha bittering is another route. Always recalculate from the new lot's alpha acid. Do not swap by weight.
Why bittering is more than arithmetic

The sum above gives you IBU. It does not tell you what the bitterness tastes like, how it lasts through the glass or why two hops at the same IBU taste different. That is hop chemistry: alpha acid fractions, oxidation products and what boil time does to them. Advanced Brewing Science teaches the mechanisms, so you can choose a bittering hop for the beer rather than for the price.
faqs: Herbal, woody and resinous, sometimes slightly spicy. In a bittering role it shows as a faint herbal finish.
How much Nugget do I need for 1,000 litres at 40 IBU?
About 1.2 kg of pellets at 13% alpha with 25% utilisation. Use your lot analysis and measured IBU to refine it.
Is Nugget a good aroma hop?
Not usually. Its oils are heavy and herbal. Most brewers use it for bittering with a light late addition at most.
Magnum is the cleanest replacement for bittering. Columbus gets closer on herbal and resinous character. Recalculate weights from the new alpha acid.
